{"success": true, "name": "extending-project-rules-docs", "description": "Extend project AGENTS.md and docs/agent-rules/ files safely.", "tags": ["docs", "agent-rules", "markdownlint", "uniwind", "conventions"], "related_skills": ["hermes-agent-skill-authoring", "plan"], "content": "---\nname: extending-project-rules-docs\ndescription: \"Extend project AGENTS.md and docs/agent-rules/ files safely.\"\nversion: 0.1.0\nauthor: phirom (phirom), Hermes Agent\nlicense: MIT\nplatforms: [linux, macos]\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [docs, agent-rules, markdownlint, uniwind, conventions]\n    related_skills: [hermes-agent-skill-authoring, plan]\n---\n\n# Extending Project Rules Docs\n\n## Overview\n\nMany mobile and web projects keep agent-rules knowledge under\n`docs/agent-rules/*.md` (file-by-file topic split) and a single\n`AGENTS.md` (always-loaded entry point). The Markdown files are subject\nto `markdownlint` with the project's default config; the entry-point\nfile is usually **protected** by the agent runtime and cannot be\nwritten to directly. This skill captures the pitfalls and workflow for\nadding or changing rules in such a repo without breaking the build or\nlosing the user's approval.\n\n## When to Use\n\n- Adding a new rule section under `docs/agent-rules/*.md`\n- Editing an existing rule section (e.g. `05-ui-conventions.md`)\n- Updating `AGENTS.md` \"always-on\" bullets to reflect new conventions\n- The user explicitly says \"write rules\" or \"document this convention\"\n\n## Don't Use For\n\n- Writing new **Hermes skills** (use `hermes-agent-skill-authoring`)\n- Writing random markdown docs not under `docs/agent-rules/`\n- Editing code that the rules describe (write code first, document the rule second)\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- Project has `yarn lint:md` (or equivalent) wired to a CI gate\n- Project has `docs/agent-rules/README.md` index file with file list\n- Project has `.markdownlint.json` (or equivalent) — read it before writing\n\n## How to Run\n\nStandard: open the project's rule file, add the section, run `yarn lint:md`,\nfix lints, commit on a docs-only branch.\n\n```bash\ncd <project>\nyarn lint:md 2>&1 | tail -20\n```\n\n## Quick Reference\n\n- `markdownlint` MD060 default is `aligned` — header column must be wider than longest data cell\n- MD032 requires a blank line before a list (between paragraph + list)\n- MD013 (line length) is usually disabled by project default\n- AGENTS.md is often **protected** by agent runtime; prepare diff in chat, ask user to apply\n- Always grep the codebase for an existing className utility before reaching for `style={{...}}`\n\n## Procedure\n\n### 1. Read the rules entry point first\n\n`AGENTS.md` is the always-loaded bridge. Read it before touching any file in `docs/agent-rules/`. Note:\n- Which files exist (the index lists them)\n- What the \"always-on\" rules say (you cannot weaken them in your docs)\n- Whether the file itself is editable from agent runtime (often NO)\n\n### 2. Read the file you plan to edit end-to-end\n\nDon't skim. Section structure, existing tables, link conventions, and \"Do / Don't\" blocks vary project-to-project. Match the tone of the surrounding prose.\n\n### 3. Plan the patch before writing it\n\nFor each table you're about to add, decide the **header word** length first. The header must be ≥ the longest data cell in its column. If unsure, pick a shorter header word (`class` instead of `className`, `code` instead of `code →`).\n\n### 4. Apply patches, then `yarn lint:md` IMMEDIATELY\n\nDo NOT write the whole section then discover five lints at the end. Apply each subsection, then run the lint. Iterate. Cost of an extra lint pass is ~5 sec; cost of an end-of-section cleanup is 5+ minutes of pattern-fiddling.\n\n### 5. For protected files (AGENTS.md), prepare the diff in chat\n\nIf the runtime blocks your write (Hermes specifically blocks `AGENTS.md` writes without user consent), show the exact diff in your reply and ask the user to apply it manually. Do not attempt workarounds — the protection is intentional.\n\n### 6. Commit on a docs-only branch\n\nA rule change is reviewable in isolation. Don't bundle with code changes.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n### Markdownlint table formatting is unforgiving\n\nMD060 default is `aligned` (pipes line up AND header column ≥ longest data cell).\nA header cell shorter than the longest data cell in the column produces\n`MD060 table pipe does not align with header for style \"aligned\"`.\n\n**Fix:** either rename the header to a shorter word, or pad with extra\ntrailing spaces to widen the header column.\n\nMD032 produces `Lists should be surrounded by blank lines` when a\nlist follows a paragraph without a blank line. Fix: add a blank line.\n\n### MD060 produces BOTH `compact` AND `aligned` errors\n\nIf you use `|---|` (compact-style divider) with no leading space, you\nget `compact` errors. If you use `| --- |` (aligned-style divider) but\nthe data column is wider than the header column, you get `aligned`\nerrors. **You cannot satisfy both at once.** Pick `aligned` (the project\ndefault) and make the header column match.\n\n### Tailwind utility classes are usually already in the codebase\n\nBefore documenting a \"use `style={{ bottom: insets.bottom + N }}`\"\nanti-pattern, **grep the codebase for existing className utilities**\nthat handle the case (e.g. `pb-safe-offset-N` on Uniwind projects).\nIf 5+ files already use a className, it is the convention — your rule\nshould reflect that, not invent a new pattern.\n\n### HeroBg screen: protected file workflow\n\nIf the agent runtime blocks writing `AGENTS.md` directly:\n- DON'T retry via `terminal`, `execute_code`, or `write_file` to `/dev/null`\n- DON'T mark the file as deleted then create a new one\n- DO show the user the exact diff in chat and ask them to apply it\n- DO continue working on the unprotected sibling files (e.g. `docs/agent-rules/*.md`)\n\n### Don't add a new rule file without updating the index\n\n`docs/agent-rules/README.md` §2 is the index. A new file under\n`docs/agent-rules/` must be added to the index in the same PR, or the\nteam won't know it exists.\n\n### Rules are knowledge; skills are work\n\nIf your \"rule\" describes a multi-step workflow with scripts and an\nartifact, it is a Skill, not a rule file. Migrate it under `.agent/skills/`\nfollowing the `hermes-agent-skill-authoring` skill conventions.\n\n## Verification\n\n- [ ] `yarn lint:md` returns 0 issues\n- [ ] `yarn tsc --noEmit` and `yarn lint` return unchanged from before\n- [ ] Any pre-commit / pre-merge hook runs green\n- [ ] If `AGENTS.md` was updated, the user manually applied the change\n- [ ] Index file updated if a new rule file was added\n- [ ] Each new rule links to its source-of-truth (the file in `docs/agent-rules/`)", "path": "software-development/extending-project-rules-docs/SKILL.md", "skill_dir": "/Users/phirom/.hermes/skills/software-development/extending-project-rules-docs", "org_provenance": null, "linked_files": null, "usage_hint": null, "required_environment_variables": [], "required_commands": [], "missing_required_environment_variables": [], "missing_credential_files": [], "missing_required_commands": [], "setup_needed": false, "setup_skipped": false, "readiness_status": "available", "_source_path": "/Users/phirom/.hermes/skills/software-development/extending-project-rules-docs/SKILL.md", "metadata": {"hermes": {"tags": ["docs", "agent-rules", "markdownlint", "uniwind", "conventions"], "related_skills": ["hermes-agent-skill-authoring", "plan"]}}}

Covers the Lynx 4.0 iOS / Android SDK corners that bite in real integration: error-payload translation, enablePreUpdateData, LynxConfigProvider fetchers, HMR/WebSocket trap, resetViewAndLayer being unsafe (use isHidden instead), CGSize.isEmpty not existing, builder.screenSize being the view frame not the screen, Android `assets.open` failing when the config plugin didn't copy the bundle, Android `LynxEnv.init` ordering, and the dev/prod URL routing split.\nlicense: MIT\n---\n\n# Embedding Lynx in an Expo / React Native App\n\nTwo scopes of skill to know about:\n- **Hermes-managed** (`~/.hermes/skills/lynx-embed-in-expo/`) — this skill. Auto-loaded by any agent on any project when the description matches.\n- **Repo-local** (`<project>/.agents/skills/expo-lynx-integration/`) — ships with the `expo-lynx` package. Has detailed `references/` files matching the `expo-module` template. If you are working inside the `expo-lynx` repo, that one is more specific; this one is the general fallback.\n\nThe two are kept in sync when relevant. Don't duplicate; reference.\n\n## What this skill covers\n\nThe `expo-lynx` package is the bridge. It hosts a `LynxView` (from `Lynx/Framework` 4.0) inside a native view, downloads the `.lynx.bundle`, and forwards engine errors to React. Android is a placeholder; iOS is where the real contract lives.\n\n## URL routing (iOS host contract)\n\n`LynxView.loadTemplate(_:withURL:initData:)` and `loadTemplateFromURL(_:initData:)` are the entry points. The host decides which based on URL scheme. Standard forms:\n\n| Form | Route | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| `https://cdn.example.com/main.lynx.bundle` | `URLSession` fetch | Prod. ATS-clean. Use `cachePolicy = .reloadRevalidatingCacheData` so CDN revalidates return 304. |\n| `http://<lan-ip>:<port>/main.lynx.bundle` | `URLSession` fetch | Dev. Requires ATS exception (`NSAllowsLocalNetworking = true` covers most LAN segments; narrow `NSExceptionDomains` if stricter). |\n| `bundle://<name>.lynx.bundle` / `<name>.lynx` | `Bundle.main.url(forResource:withExtension:)` | Static. Strip the `bundle://` prefix first. |\n| `file://…` | Read bytes via `Data(contentsOf:options:)` | Local file URL. |\n\nThe routing logic lives in the host's `loadSource` (ExpoLynxView.swift:97). Mirror that branch order when writing your own host.\n\n## The four iOS Lynx SDK details that bit me in real integration\n\nThese are the four corners the SDK docs skip. Save them.\n\n### 1. `enablePreUpdateData` is OFF by default\n\n`LynxView.h:195-197`: \"Normally, updateData before loadTemplate does not take effect. If you want to cache the data updated before loadTemplate and use it together when loadTemplate, please set `EnablePreUpdateData` option in `LynxViewBuilder`.\"\n\nIf your React host passes `initialData` to the bridge and the data arrives *before* `url` is set (different prop, prop-order races, async setters), the data is silently dropped unless you flip this on:\n\n```swift\nbuilder.insertLynxViewConfig(true, forKey: \"enablePreUpdateData\")\n```\n\nConfirmed working on Lynx 4.0. Without it, the bug is silent — no error, no log, just a render with empty `useInitData()`.\n\n### 2. `LynxConfig(provider: nil)` has no resource fetchers\n\n`LynxConfig` accepts a `LynxConfigProvider?`. Passing `nil` makes the engine fall back to its default no-op provider. The default provider has no image fetcher, no generic resource fetcher, no log service. Your `LynxView` will render text and primitives fine, but:\n- `loadImage()` returns nothing.\n- Any generic resource request (custom URL schemes inside the bundle) silently 404s.\n- Engine logs `enableGenericResourceFetcher: false` once at startup. That's the diagnostic.\n\nFor any non-trivial page you need at least `LynxImageFetcher`. See `explorer/darwin/ios/lynx_explorer/LynxExplorer/LynxViewShellViewController.m:395-397` for the canonical three-fetcher wiring (`genericResourceFetcher`, `templateResourceFetcher`, `mediaResourceFetcher`).\n\n### 3. `LynxViewLifecycle` vs `LynxViewLifecycleV2`\n\nBoth protocols live in `platform/darwin/common/lynx/public/`:\n- `LynxViewClient.h:48` — legacy. All `@optional`. Has `lynxView:didLoadFinishedWithUrl:`, `lynxView:didRecieveError:`, `lynxViewDidStartLoading:`, `lynxViewDidFirstScreen:`.\n- `LynxViewClientV2.h:60` — adds `onPageStartedWithLynxView:withPipelineInfo:` (pipeline info: URL + pipeline origin) and `onResourceLoaded:` (per-resource error reporting).\n\n`LynxView.addLifecycleClient:` accepts both. The Explorer uses V2 to track per-resource loads; the `expo-lynx` host uses legacy because it only needs `didLoadFinishedWithUrl:` + `didRecieveError:`. Choose legacy when you only need page-level events; switch to V2 when you need per-resource error reporting or pre-load setup hooks.\n\n### 4. Swift rename: `updateData(with:)` → `updateDataWithTemplateData:`\n\nThe Swift importer maps `- (void)updateDataWithTemplateData:(nullable LynxTemplateData*)data;` to `func updateData(with: LynxTemplateData?)`. So in Swift:\n\n```swift\nlynxView.updateData(with: templateData)   // correct\nlynxView.updateDataWithTemplateData(templateData)  // also works, less idiomatic\n```\n\nSame for the other `updateDataWith*:` variants.\n\n## The 201 error and the HMR / WebSocketModule trap\n\nSymptom in the host: `LynxErrorEventPayload { code: \"201\", message: \"The operation couldn't be completed. (com.lynx.error error 201.)\" }`. The host's `didRecieveError` is hit.\n\nRoot cause in practice: the embedded iOS Lynx runtime 4.0 does **not** ship `LynxWebSocketModule`. The `rspeedy dev` bundle includes `@lynx-js/webpack-dev-transport` which calls `new WebSocket(...)` at module-top-level inside `.rspeedy/main/background.js`. That throws `Error: WebSocket is not found. Please use Lynx >= 2.16 or consider using a polyfill.` synchronously during `LoadScript`, which the engine surfaces as 201.\n\nFix in the bundle source's `lynx.config.ts`:\n\n```ts\n// lynx.config.ts (the bundle source project, NOT the host app)\nexport default defineConfig({\n  environments: {\n    lynx: {\n      dev: {\n        // ponytail: embedded iOS Lynx doesn't ship LynxWebSocketModule;\n        // turning HMR/live-reload off stops webpack-dev-transport from throwing.\n        hmr: false,\n        liveReload: false,\n      },\n    },\n  },\n});\n```\n\nYou lose live-reload inside the view. To re-add it: register a native `LynxWebSocketModule` in the host that wraps `URLSessionWebSocketTask`, then flip the flags back on. 30-line Swift class + Obj-C `LynxModule` conformance.\n\n## CDP debugging vs rspeedy HMR — they are different channels\n\nThe two are easy to confuse because both use WebSockets. They are not.\n\n| Channel | Purpose | Transport | Pods |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Lynx DevTools (CDP) | Remote inspector, manual reload, console, breakpoints via the Lynx Debugger app | SocketRocket-based LynxWebSocket inside the LynxDevtool framework, served by LynxDevToolService. Auto-registers via the @LynxServiceRegister macro on +load | LynxDevtool, LynxService/Devtool, SocketRocket |\n| rspeedy HMR | Pushes hot updates from pnpm dev to a running page. The bundle's @lynx-js/webpack-dev-transport calls new WebSocket and expects a LynxWebSocketModule on the engine side | Engine user-JS WebSocket module (separate from DevTool). Not shipped by the embedded runtime | None on host side |\n\nLynxDevToolService and LynxWebSocket (in lynx_devtool/) are the CDP stack. They are NOT the rspeedy HMR transport.\n\nFor DevTools-only integration (inspect + manual reload), the integration is small. Verified against the explorer reference:\n\n- Add to Podfile or podspec: `LynxDevtool 4.0.0`, `LynxService/Devtool 4.0.0`, `SocketRocket ~> 0.6`.\n- In `OnCreate` after `LynxEnv.sharedInstance()`:\n  - `DevToolSettings.sharedInstance().bootstrap.applyDevelopmentDefaultsIfUnset()` — sets `lynxDebugEnabled` + `logBoxEnabled` defaults if not already set.\n  - `LynxService(LynxServiceDevToolProtocol.self).enableAllSessions()` — turns the service on for every `LynxView`.\n  - Do NOT call `LynxServiceCenter.inst().registerService(LynxDevToolService.sharedInstance())` — auto-registered by the `@LynxServiceRegister` macro on `+load`. A double register is a no-op at best, a duplicate-init at worst.\n\nFor rspeedy HMR inside the embedded view, the host-side fix is to add a `LynxWebSocketModule` stub. The DevTools integration above does NOT enable rspeedy HMR.\n\n## The lost-cause error message problem\n\nThe bridge was originally forwarding only `nsError.localizedDescription` to React, which collapsed every Lynx error to `The operation couldn't be completed. (com.lynx.error error 201.)`. Fix: read the NSError userInfo chain — `NSUnderlyingErrorKey` first, then `reason`, `NSDebugDescriptionErrorKey`, `NSLocalizedDescriptionKey`. After the fix, the host surfaces the actual `rawError.message` and stack. Patch recipe in the repo-local skill's `references/error-payload.md`.\n\n## Three more corners the docs skip\n\n### 5. Hide the view on load failure — *do not* call `resetViewAndLayer`\n\nWhen a load fails (HTTP 404, network error, source-not-found), the Lynx engine does *not* clear the previously rendered template. The old bundle keeps painting under whatever error overlay you show. Symptom: user switches Dev → Prod, prod 404s, but the dev bundle's UI is still on screen.\n\n**Wrong fix:** `lynxView.resetViewAndLayer()` (`LynxView.h:112`). The implementation (`LynxView.mm:159-170`) iterates and removes subviews but does *not* reset `_templateRender`. The engine's element tree, animation state, and module handles still reference those views. Calling it on a live `_templateRender` (mid-load or after a successful load) crashes with a UIView assertion. Verified by reading the impl, not guessed.\n\n**Right fix:** toggle visibility only. On the iOS host, `lynxView.isHidden = true` in the host's `finishWithError` path and the synchronous `source-not-found` branch of `loadSource`; `lynxView.isHidden = false` at the top of `loadSource`. On the Android host, `lynxView.visibility = View.GONE` on `onReceivedError`, `View.VISIBLE` on `loadBundle` and `onLoadSuccess`. Pair with a `hasLoadedTemplate = false` flag so the next successful load re-arms the live-update gate.\n\nDo **not** call reset/hide in `didRecieveError` / `onReceivedError` *after* a successful load — that would blank the page on a JS warning. The engine reports engine-side errors via that callback and expects to keep showing the page.\n\n### 6. `CGSize` has no `.isEmpty`\n\n`CGRect.isEmpty` exists; `CGSize` does not. `bounds.size.isEmpty` compiles in some Xcodes and crashes in the strict-build one — the symptom is `value of type 'CGSize' has no member 'isEmpty'`. Use `bounds.size.width > 0 && bounds.size.height > 0` instead. Same trap applies to any other `CGSize` field.\n\n### 7. `LynxViewBuilder.screenSize` is the view's drawing frame, not the screen\n\n`LynxBaseConfigurator.h:78-81`: `screenSize` is in **points**, and represents the Lynx view's drawing frame — *not* `UIScreen.main.bounds.size`. The explorer reference (`LynxViewShellViewController.m:386`) sets it from the Lynx view's `frame.size` after subtracting safe area. Passing the full screen (including safe area + status bar) makes CSS `vh` / `vw` / `rpx` resolve against the device screen rather than the embedded view.\n\nLazy default: **don't set it**. Engine falls back to its own defaults. If you actually use `vh`/`vw`/`rpx` in the Lynx page, call `lynxView.updateScreenMetricsWithWidth:height:` (`LynxView.h:262`) from inside your layout-update path with the view bounds. Don't bother setting it in the builder — the builder value is only used as an init-time hint, and `updateScreenMetrics` overrides it.\n\n### 8. UX pattern: human-readable errors in dev, blank in prod\n\nThe bridge already forwards `nativeEvent.code` + `nativeEvent.message`. In `App.tsx` (the host's host) you want:\n\n- **Dev / static**: render an overlay with a friendly description; hide the stale Lynx view (`opacity: 0`) so the overlay is readable.\n- **Prod**: render nothing. Just `lynxView.isHidden = true` (native side) + the status text. Don't show a stack trace to end users.\n\nPattern: a small lookup table keyed by `nativeEvent.code` (HTTP codes 404/403/500 + engine codes 201/102 + your own custom error strings like `ERR_LYNX_SOURCE_NOT_FOUND`) that maps to one-line descriptions. Fall back to `nativeEvent.message` for anything you haven't seen. Reset overlay state on `selectSource` so retries start clean.\n\n```ts\nconst KNOWN_ERRORS: Record<string, string> = {\n  '404': 'Bundle not found on the server (HTTP 404).',\n  ERR_LYNX_SOURCE_NOT_FOUND: 'No Lynx bundle is bundled with the app for static.',\n  '201': 'Lynx engine threw a JavaScript / runtime error (code 201).',\n};\nfunction describeLynxError(code: string | number, message: string): string {\n  return KNOWN_ERRORS[String(code)] ?? message;\n}\n```\n\nKeep the table local to the example app — it is a UX choice, not engine contract.\n\n## Android host parity\n\nThe Android port in `expo-lynx/android/src/main/java/expo/modules/lynx/` mirrors the iOS contract. Four Android-specific corners that don't apply to iOS:\n\n### 9. Config plugin must copy bundled resources to Android assets too\n\niOS config plugins handle `Bundle.main` resource registration; Android requires a manual copy into `android/app/src/main/assets/`. Skip this and the static-bundle load throws `LynxErrorCodeLoadTemplate` (102, sub_code 10203) — `appContext.assets.open(uri)` returns `FileNotFoundException`.\n\nThe `expo-lynx` plugin uses `withDangerousMod(config, ['android', …])` to copy each `bundledResources` entry into the assets directory before Gradle packages them. Run `npx expo prebuild` after changing the plugin.\n\n### 10. `LynxViewClient` is the Android equivalent of `LynxViewLifecycle`\n\n`com.lynx.tasm.LynxViewClient` exposes `onLoadSuccess()`, `onReceivedError(LynxError)`, etc. Add it via `lynxView.addLynxViewClient(client)`. `LynxError` is a Java/Kotlin class, not Obj-C — public getters: `getErrorCode()` (Int), `getSubCode()` (Int), `getMsg()` (full JSON string), `getSummaryMessage()`, `getType()`, `getLevel()`, `getFixSuggestion()`, `getRootCause()`. There's no public `getCallStack()`; the stack lives inside `getMsg()`'s JSON.\n\nWire `onReceivedError` to forward the same payload shape iOS uses (`{ url, code, message, subCode, type, level, fixSuggestion, rootCause, json }`) so JS doesn't need a platform branch. Default to `summaryMessage.ifEmpty { msg }` for the human-readable `message`.\n\n### 11. `LynxEnv.inst().init(application, null, null, null)` must run before any `LynxView` is built\n\n`LynxViewBuilder().build(context)` requires `LynxEnv` initialized first. Do this in the module's `OnCreate` block — Expo Modules Core runs `OnCreate` exactly once per module instance. Don't put it in the view's `init` (the view's init runs once per view instance; the env is process-singleton).\n\nRegister `LynxHttpService` + `LynxLogService` via `LynxServiceCenter.inst().registerService(...)` before `init`. Skip image service registration for the demo; add a Coil-backed `ILynxImageService` later if the bundle references images.\n\n### 12. `shouldUseAndroidLayout = true` on the view\n\n`ExpoView` defaults to React Native's Yoga-driven measurement. The LynxView child needs Android's layout system to measure it directly; otherwise it gets `MATCH_PARENT × MATCH_PARENT` LayoutParams but is never measured, and the screen stays blank even though Lynx is running. Override the property in the view's body.\n\n### 13. Android asset URI normalization\n\n`AbsTemplateProvider.loadTemplate(uri)` receives the `src` string verbatim. For asset lookups, use the raw filename (e.g. `\"static.lynx\"`) — Android's `AssetManager.open` resolves it as a relative path under `assets/`. Don't prefix with `bundle://` on Android; that's an iOS host convention.\n\n## Common errors table\n\n| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |\n|---|---|---|\n| Code 201, generic NSError message | Engine-side JS exception. Original bridge flattens NSError → loses cause. | Xcode console for the underlying `Lynx error` line — it has `rawError.message` and stack. Apply the errorPayload patch. |\n| Code 201, `Error: WebSocket is not found` | HMR/live-reload bundle tried to open a WS; embedded runtime has no WS module. | `hmr: false, liveReload: false` in `lynx.config.ts` environments.lynx.dev. |\n| HTTP 200 bundle but blank page | Engine version mismatch. `engine_version` in the bundle header must be ≤ the host's Lynx SDK. | Rebuild bundle with matching `@lynx-js/rspeedy`; re-export `lynx_core.js` for the host. |\n| ATS cleartext error in Xcode console | `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = false` and no LAN exception. | `NSAllowsLocalNetworking = true` (broad) or `NSExceptionDomains` (narrow). |\n| `LynxErrorCodeLoadTemplate` (102) | Bundle bytes corrupt or truncated. | `curl -I` and compare `Content-Length` to the build artifact. |\n| Bundle loads but page is blank, no console | `initialData` shape doesn't match page's `useInitData` expectations. | Page-side bug, not the bridge. |\n| Data set before URL silently dropped | `enablePreUpdateData` not set. | `builder.insertLynxViewConfig(true, forKey: \"enablePreUpdateData\")`. |\n| Failed reload shows the *previous* bundle | Engine doesn't auto-clear on load failure. `resetViewAndLayer` is unsafe — toggle `lynxView.isHidden` / `View.GONE` instead. | `lynxView.isHidden = true` (iOS) or `lynxView.visibility = View.GONE` (Android) in the host's `finishWithError` / `onReceivedError` and the source-not-found branch; toggle back at the top of `loadSource`. |\n| Android static bundle fails with code 102, sub_code 10203 | `assets.open(uri)` returned `FileNotFoundException` — bundled resource was not copied into `android/app/src/main/assets/`. | Config plugin must call `withDangerousMod(['android', …])` to copy each `bundledResources` entry; run `npx expo prebuild`. |\n| `nativeEvent.code` is `201` and `message` is the generic NSError translation | Original bridge collapsed the chain. | Apply the `errorPayload` patch; surface `rawError.message` from Xcode console. |\n| App shows `com.lynx.error error 201.` to end users | No human-readable mapping; bridge forwards the literal NSError. | Add a `describeLynxError(code, message)` lookup table in `App.tsx`; show a friendly overlay in dev/static, blank in prod. |\n| Build error: `CGSize has no member isEmpty` | Copy-pasted `CGRect.isEmpty` idiom onto a `CGSize`. | Use `bounds.size.width > 0 && bounds.size.height > 0`. |\n| CSS `vh`/`vw`/`rpx` slightly off in embedded view | `builder.screenSize = UIScreen.main.bounds.size` includes safe area. | Drop it; call `updateScreenMetricsWithWidth:height:` from layout with view size. |\n| Crash inside Lynx error path on stale-render fix | Called `resetViewAndLayer` — engine asserts when subviews are torn out from under `_templateRender`. | Use `isHidden` / `View.GONE` instead; only the Lynx engine can safely clear its render tree. |\n\n## Quick checklist for a fresh integration\n\n- [ ] Bundle source's `lynx.config.ts` has `hmr: false, liveReload: false` under `environments.lynx.dev`.\n- [ ] Host's `LynxViewBuilder` block sets `enablePreUpdateData: true`.\n- [ ] Host Info.plist has `NSAllowsLocalNetworking = true` (or narrower exception) for LAN dev URL.\n- [ ] `LynxView.url` is parameterized via build config (`expo-constants` `extra.*` if Expo).\n- [ ] `onError` handler reads `nativeEvent.code` and `nativeEvent.message` and logs both — Xcode console for the underlying stack.\n- [ ] For prod: CDN URL is HTTPS, content-hashed, cache-control permits revalidation.\n- [ ] If page needs images / network resources: implement `LynxImageFetcher` (minimum) and pass a real `LynxConfigProvider`.\n- [ ] Android host: `LynxEnv.inst().init(...)` in module `OnCreate`, before any `LynxView` is built.\n- [ ] Android host: config plugin copies `bundledResources` into `android/app/src/main/assets/` via `withDangerousMod`.\n- [ ] Android host: `ExpoLynxView` overrides `shouldUseAndroidLayout = true`.\n- [ ] Want Lynx DevTools (CDP) debugging: add `LynxDevtool` + `LynxService/Devtool` + `SocketRocket` deps; in `OnCreate` call `DevToolSettings.sharedInstance().bootstrap.applyDevelopmentDefaultsIfUnset()` + `LynxService(LynxServiceDevToolProtocol.self).enableAllSessions()`. Do NOT manually call `registerService` on `LynxDevToolService` — auto-registered.\n\n## Project-local vs Hermes-managed skill: where to look first\n\n- **Inside the `expo-lynx` repo**: load `expo-lynx-integration` from `.agents/skills/`. Has detailed `references/` matching the `expo-module` template.\n- **On any other project**: this skill (`lynx-embed-in-expo`) is the fallback. {"success": true, "name": "embed-native-ui-engine-as-expo-module", "description": "Embed a Lynx-style engine as a React Native/Expo native view.", "tags": [], "related_skills": [], "content": "---\nname: embed-native-ui-engine-as-expo-module\ndescription: Embed a Lynx-style engine as a React Native/Expo native view.\n---\n\n# Embed a Native UI Engine as a React Native / Expo Native View\n\nEnd-to-end playbook for wrapping a third-party native UI engine (Lynx, Weex, future ByteDance/JS-engine surfaces) in a React Native or Expo Modules native view, exposing it as a `<LynxView>`/`<EngineView>` component to RN/Expo JS, and shipping a debug-build demo APK to an Android emulator.\n\nThe class of work: take an engine that ships native `.so` files + a JS bundle format, wire it into React Native's native-view bridge (plain RN `ViewManager`/`RCTViewManager` or Expo Modules), surface load/error events to JS, and produce a runnable build. Most of the gotchas live in the bridge layer, not the engine.\n\n## When to Use\n\n- Building an Expo Module that hosts a Lynx / Weex / WebView-as-engine surface inside an RN/Expo app\n- Adding `onLoad` / `onError` (and similar lifecycle) events to a native view module\n- Diagnosing an Expo module that compiles, the JS bundle loads, but the screen is blank and `uiautomator dump` shows no children\n- Migrating from old `Events(\"...\") { ... sendEvent(...) }` DSL to the new `View.EventDispatcher()` property-delegate pattern\n- Shipping a release APK that bundles a third-party `.bundle` asset alongside the JS bundle\n\n## When NOT to Use\n\n- The user wants to choose between mini-app architectures (Re.Pack vs Lynx vs WebView) — that's `react-native-mini-app-architecture`\n- Building a pure native module (no UI, just methods) — the Expo native-module-tutorial covers it; this skill assumes a view with bundle loading\n- Adding Lynx 4.0 support to a brand-new codebase that has no Expo Modules infrastructure yet — start with the Expo native-view tutorial first\n- iOS-only or web-only paths — this skill is Android-first because the documented Lynx + Coil + Fresco interaction is Android-specific\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- Expo SDK 49+ with `@react-native/gradle-plugin` and `expo-modules-core` 1.5+\n- Uniwind or NativeWind for styling (any RN UI lib works)\n- Lynx 4.0+ from `org.lynxsdk.lynx` (or analogous third-party engine — substitute the imports)\n- A `lynx-source/`-style project producing `.lynx.bundle` files\n- An Android emulator (Pixel-class AVD with arm64-v8a system image)\n- `ANDROID_HOME` set; `adb` reachable\n\n## When to Read the Linked Reference\n\nThe `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` file captures the non-obvious gotchas that came up building this on Lynx 4.0:\n\n- The `shouldUseAndroidLayout = true` override that makes the screen actually paint\n- The Coil-vs-Fresco dependency choice (RN 0.86's bundled Fresco conflicts with Lynx's reference image service)\n- The `Vararg allowed only inside a parenthesized argument list` Kotlin DSL trap\n- `findAppContextOrNull` does NOT exist on `ExpoView`; suppress `ViewConstructor` lint instead of fabricating `AppContext`\n- `View.EventDispatcher()` vs the old manual `Events() { ... sendEvent(...) }` DSL\n- Dev-mode rspeedy bundles require a WebSocket HMR endpoint; always pass `--mode production` for asset bundling\n- iOS Swift class/property name mapping is UNVERIFIED against the actual Lynx 4.0 pod — gotchas #17 tables the names most likely to fail compile\n- `expo-module.config.json` `apple.modules` must match `@objc(...)` annotation string — gotchas #18\n- iOS image service auto-registers via `LynxService/Image` pod `+load`; do NOT add explicit wiring for symmetry with Android — gotchas #19\n\n`references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` is the iOS counterpart: the embed-guide sizing requirement (`layoutWidthMode` / `layoutHeightMode` are mandatory), ObjC interop (only `LynxViewClient` requires `@objc`), the asset-bundle shipping path (Xcode \"Copy Bundle Resources\", not Gradle AAR merger), and why the iOS image service is intentionally left without an explicit `LynxImageService.sharedInstance()` registration.\n\n`references/image-service-lifecycle.md` covers register/replace/remove decisions for the ILynxImageService SPI on Android (Coil is the only viable backend given RN 0.86's Fresco conflict).\n\nThe `references/pnpm-monorepo-layout.md` covers the `apps/<app>` + `packages/<engine>-view` workspace split when the engine needs a sibling package. Includes the `.npmrc` `node-linker=hoisted` requirement, autolinking `searchPaths` shape, cross-package Gradle wiring, and the anti-pattern of splitting out an image service as its own workspace package (the user explicitly rejected that pattern).\n\nThe `templates/serve-bundle.js` is a ready-to-copy Express static server for the engine's `.bundle` file during dev iteration (Android emulator's host-loopback `10.0.2.2:3000`). Drop it into `apps/demo/scripts/`, replace `<engine>` with the package name, run `node scripts/serve-bundle.js`.\n\nRead each the first time you hit any of those errors. The skill below tells you which symptom maps to which gotcha.\n\n## Procedure\n\n### Step 0 — If the user asks for plain React Native, first check whether a bridge already exists\n\nBefore writing bridge code, grep the target checkout for existing RN surfaces:\n\n```bash\ngrep -R \"com.facebook.react\\|RCTViewManager\\|RCTViewComponentView\\|ReactPackage\\|requireNativeComponent\\|codegenNativeComponent\\|expo-modules-core\\|requireNativeView\" -n .\n```\n\nIf there is no existing bridge, do not touch Lynx core. Wrap the host APIs that already exist:\n\n- Android: `LynxEnv.inst().init(...)`, `LynxViewBuilder`, `LynxView`, `renderTemplateWithBaseUrl(...)` / `renderTemplateUrl(...)`, `destroy()`.\n- iOS: `[LynxEnv.sharedInstance prepareConfig:]`, `[[LynxView alloc] initWithBuilderBlock:]`, `loadTemplate:withURL:initData:` / `loadTemplateFromURL:initData:`, explicit `layoutWidthMode` / `layoutHeightMode` sizing.\n\nFor a first PR, expose only `src`, optional `initData`, `onLoad`, `onError`, and `style`. Skip message bridge, Node-API addon, DevTool, custom modules, caching, and multi-bundle routing until one real Lynx bundle paints inside an RN screen.\n\n### Step 1 — Build the Kotlin module skeleton\n\n**File:** `modules/<engine>-view/android/build.gradle`\n\n```groovy\nplugins {\n  id 'com.android.library'\n  id 'expo-module-gradle-plugin'\n}\nandroid { namespace \"expo.modules.<engine>view\" }\ndependencies {\n  implementation \"org.<vendor>:<engine>:4.0.0\"   // or equivalent\n}\n```\n\n**File:** `modules/<engine>-view/expo-module.config.json`\n\n```json\n{ \"platforms\": [\"android\"], \"android\": { \"modules\": [\"expo.modules.<engine>view.<Engine>ViewModule\"] } }\n```\n\n**No `package.json` is required at the module root.** Expo Modules autolinking discovers the native side via `expo-module.config.json`. Metro resolves the JS entry by direct path (`import { X } from \"./modules/<engine>-view/src\"`).\n\n### Step 2 — Write the View class\n\n```kotlin\n@Suppress(\"ViewConstructor\")\nclass ExpoLynxView(context: Context, appContext: AppContext) : ExpoView(context, appContext) {\n\n  // *** Critical: opt into Android's layout system. ***\n  // Without this, ExpoView's default behavior (shouldUseAndroidLayout = false)\n  // means the child native view never gets measured by Android's measure/layout\n  // pass, even though Lynx reports load/layout success in logs. Result:\n  // blank screen, uiautomator dump shows only FrameLayout/LinearLayout,\n  // no ExpoLynxView children. Setting this to true triggers post-layout\n  // re-measurement. Reference: github.com/facebook/react-native/issues/17968\n  override val shouldUseAndroidLayout: Boolean = true\n\n  private val lynxView: LynxView = LynxViewBuilder()\n    .setTemplateProvider(LynxTemplateProvider(context))\n    .addBehaviors(XElementBehaviors().create())\n    .build(context)\n\n  // Use property delegates — NOT manual Events() { ... } blocks.\n  // Old DSL (broken in Expo Modules Core 1.6+):\n  //   Events(\"onLoad\") { view -> view.onLoad = { sendEvent(\"onLoad\") } }\n  //   // → \"Passing value as a vararg is allowed only inside a parenthesized argument list\"\n  private val onLoad by EventDispatcher<Unit>()\n  private val onError by EventDispatcher<MutableMap<String, Any?>>()\n\n  init {\n    lynxView.layoutParams = ViewGroup.LayoutParams(MATCH_PARENT, MATCH_PARENT)\n    addView(lynxView)\n    lynxView.addLynxViewClient(object : LynxViewClient() {\n      override fun onLoadSuccess() { onLoad.invoke(Unit) }\n      override fun onReceivedError(error: LynxError) {\n        onError.invoke(mutableMapOf(\n          \"message\" to (if (error.summaryMessage.isNotEmpty()) error.summaryMessage else error.msg),\n          \"code\" to error.errorCode,\n          \"subCode\" to error.subCode,\n          // ... etc — see references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md for the full map\n        ))\n      }\n    })\n  }\n}\n```\n\n**Completion criterion:** `ExpoLynxView.kt` extends `ExpoView`, has `shouldUseAndroidLayout = true`, exposes `EventDispatcher<T>` properties, attaches a `LynxViewClient`.\n\n### Step 3 — Write the Module class (thin glue)\n\n```kotlin\nclass LynxViewModule : Module() {\n  override fun definition() = ModuleDefinition {\n    Name(\"ExpoLynxView\")\n    View(ExpoLynxView::class) {\n      Prop(\"src\") { view: ExpoLynxView, src: String -> view.loadBundle(src) }\n      Events(\"onLoad\", \"onError\")   // NO body — registration only\n    }\n    OnCreate { /* register image service, init LynxEnv */ }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n**Completion criterion:** `Events(...)` takes no body. Prop wiring goes through the view's exposed methods, not through `sendEvent` in the DSL.\n\n### Step 4 — Write the JS surface\n\n```ts\n// src/LynxView.types.ts\nexport type LynxErrorEvent = {\n  message: string;\n  code: number; subCode: number; type: number; level: string;\n  fixSuggestion: string; rootCause: string; json: string;\n} & Record<string, unknown>;\n\nexport type LynxViewProps = {\n  src: string;\n  onLoad?: (event: { nativeEvent: { url: string } }) => void;\n  onError?: (event: { nativeEvent: LynxErrorEvent }) => void;\n} & Omit<ViewProps, 'style' | 'children'>;\n\n// src/LynxView.tsx\nimport { requireNativeView } from 'expo';\nconst NativeLynxView = requireNativeView<React.ComponentType<LynxViewProps>>('ExpoLynxView');\nexport default function LynxView(props: LynxViewProps) {\n  return <NativeLynxView {...props} />;\n}\n\n// src/index.ts\nexport { default as LynxView } from './LynxView';\nexport * from './LynxView.types';\n```\n\n**Completion criterion:** JS handlers receive `{ nativeEvent: payload }`, not bare payload. The `LynxViewProps` type extends `ViewProps` so consumers get `testID`, `accessibilityLabel`, `ref` for free.\n\n### Step 5 — Build the JS-side asset\n\n```bash\ncd lynx-source/\nnpx rspeedy build --mode production    # *** NOT just `build` ***\n\ncp dist/main.lynx.bundle \\\n  /path/to/lynx-expo-demo/modules/<engine>-view/android/src/main/assets/main.<engine>.bundle\n```\n\n`--mode production` is the difference between a 279 KB standalone bundle and a 1.6 MB dev bundle that requires a WebSocket HMR endpoint. Dev-mode bundles fail at runtime with `Error: WebSocket is not found. Please use Lynx >= 2.16`.\n\niOS ships the same bundle via Xcode's \"Copy Bundle Resources\" build phase in the host app's target (one-time setup per project — see `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` for the step-by-step). The dev-server URL path (`<LynxView src=\"http://<host>:3000/...\">`) bypasses both copy steps.\n\n### Step 6 — Build and install on Android\n\n```bash\nexport ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Library/Android/sdk\ncd /path/to/lynx-expo-demo/\nnpx expo prebuild --clean              # one-time, regenerates android/\ncd android && ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease\n\n# Install on a wiped emulator — see Pitfalls for why wipe is needed\nadb -s emulator-5554 shell pm clear com.phirom.<pkg> 2>/dev/null   # optional\nadb -s emulator-5554 install -r app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk\nadb -s emulator-5554 shell monkey -p com.phirom.<pkg> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1\n```\n\n**Completion criterion:** APK installs cleanly, app launches, logcat shows `OnPatchFinishForFiber` and `Layout finish with result size: <screen-size>` within 5 seconds of launch.\n\n### Step 7 — Verify the rendered UI\n\nDon't trust logcat alone. `OnPatchFinishForFiber` can fire while the screen is blank. Verify with:\n\n```bash\n# UI hierarchy — must contain ScrollView or HorizontalScrollView\nadb -s emulator-5554 shell uiautomator dump /sdcard/ui.xml\nadb -s emulator-5554 pull /sdcard/ui.xml /tmp/ui.xml\ngrep -oE 'class=\"[^\"]+\"' /tmp/ui.xml | sort -u\n# Should include: android.widget.ScrollView, android.widget.HorizontalScrollView\n\n# Pixel content — if mean is ~65000 out of 65535, screen is blank white\nidentify -format '%[mean]' /tmp/screencap.png\n# A working app has mean ~50000-62000 depending on background color\n```\n\n### Step 7a — Diagnose \"iOS module didn't link\" before you blame the Swift code\n\nWhen `pod install` runs clean but your module's pod is missing from `Podfile.lock`, or `use_expo_modules!` doesn't pick it up, the cause is usually in the autolinking layer, not your Swift. Run the three diagnostic commands in order — they form a pipeline that narrows the failure to one of: resolver, config filter, podspec gate.\n\n```bash\n# 1. Does Expo's resolver see the package?\n#    (Note: iOS uses --platform apple, NOT --platform ios.)\nnode --no-warnings --eval \"require('expo/bin/autolinking')\" \\\n  expo-modules-autolinking resolve --json --platform apple \\\n  | grep -oE '\"packageName\":\"[^\"]*<name>[^\"]*\"'\n\n# 2. Does the Podfile-equivalent config command return the pod?\n#    This is what `use_expo_modules!` actually runs. Different filter\n#    than (1) — passing (1) but failing here means the JSON contract\n#    doesn't include the field `use_expo_modules!` needs (podName /\n#    podspecDir / pods[]).\nnode --no-warnings --eval \"require('expo/bin/autolinking')\" \\\n  expo-modules-autolinking react-native-config --json --platform ios \\\n  | grep -i \"<name>\"\n\n# 3. Why does `use_expo_modules!` skip it?\n#    `--verbose` surfaces the actual rejection line that plain\n#    `pod install` hides. The typical messages:\ncd ios && pod install --verbose 2>&1 | grep -i \"<name>\"\n#    - \"<name> doesn't support iOS platform\"\n#         → podspec's `s.platforms = { :ios => 'X.Y' }` is HIGHER than\n#           the app's `ios.deploymentTarget` in Podfile.properties.json.\n#           Bump the deployment target to match the podspec (or\n#           downgrade the podspec). This is the most common cause.\n#    - \"Missing required attribute authors/homepage/source\"\n#         → podspec is missing one of those three keys. Add them.\n#    - no output at all\n#         → resolver didn't return the package; check (1) and (2).\n```\n\nThe (1)→(2)→(3) cascade pinpoints whether the problem is: package not discovered (1), JSON shape wrong (2), or podspec rejected (3). Each fix is small and local. Don't rewrite Swift or podspecs until the cascade names the layer that's actually failing.\n\nThe same cascade works for Android — substitute `--platform android` for (1), and check `node_modules/<name>/android/build.gradle` instead of `pod install` for (3).\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n| Symptom | Cause | Fix |\n|---|---|---|\n| Blank white screen, logcat shows `OnPatchFinishForFiber` + `Layout finish` for full screen size | `shouldUseAndroidLayout` not overridden | Add `override val shouldUseAndroidLayout: Boolean = true` |\n| Kotlin compile error: `Passing value as a vararg is allowed only inside a parenthesized argument list` at `sendEvent(\"...\", error)` | Used the old DSL `Events(\"...\") { view -> ... sendEvent(...) }` pattern | Use `Events(\"onError\")` (no body) in the module DSL; define `private val onError by EventDispatcher<...>()` in the view |\n| `Cannot find symbol: findAppContextOrNull` | Tried to fabricate `AppContext` from a bare `Context` — the helper doesn't exist on `ExpoView` | Don't add the `(Context, AttributeSet)` constructor. Add `@Suppress(\"ViewConstructor\")` at the class level instead. |\n| Build fails with `Cannot resolve symbol LynxError` or wrong method signatures | Using a private `mSummaryMessage` / `mCallStack` Java field that has no public Kotlin getter | Only read fields that have public getters: `summaryMessage`, `getMsg()`, `getErrorCode()`, `getSubCode()`, `getType()`, `getLevel()`, `getFixSuggestion()`, `getRootCause()`. Don't read `callStack` — it's not exposed. |\n| iOS Swift files don't compile / crash at link time | Lynx 4.0 ObjC class/property names in Swift don't match the inferred Swift names | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #17 for the table of names that may need fixing against `LynxView.h` / `LynxError.h`. The iOS scaffolding in this repo is UNVERIFIED — verify on a real Mac with Xcode before trusting it. |\n| iOS module class not registered at runtime — ExpoModulesProvider.swift doesn't list it | `apple.modules` in `expo-module.config.json` doesn't match the `@objc(...)` annotation on the Swift class | See gotchas #18. Match the string exactly. Also re-run `expo prebuild --clean && pod install` — a stale `ExpoModulesProvider.swift` is a common silent cause. |\n| `pod install` clean but module missing from `Podfile.lock` / `use_expo_modules!` prints `<name> doesn't support iOS platform` | Podspec's `s.platforms = { :ios => 'X.Y' }` is HIGHER than the app's `ios.deploymentTarget` in `Podfile.properties.json` (Expo scaffold default = `15.1`, many third-party pods require `16.4`+) | Run the diagnostic cascade from Step 7a to confirm which layer rejected the pod. Then either bump `ios.deploymentTarget` to match the podspec, or downgrade the podspec. Note: bumping the deployment target raises the App Store minimum OS — check that's acceptable. |\n| Reviewer adds `LynxServiceCenter.register(LynxImageService.sharedInstance())` to iOS \"for symmetry\" with Android | Doesn't realize the `LynxService/Image` pod auto-registers via `+load` | See gotchas #19. The Android ↔ iOS asymmetry is intentional; add a code comment explaining why there's no explicit iOS call so future readers don't \"fix\" it. |\n| `CLEARTEXT communication to <IP> not permitted by network security policy` | Image URLs use `http://` and Android 9+ blocks cleartext by default | Either use HTTPS for image URLs, or add `android:usesCleartextTraffic=\"true\"` to `AndroidManifest.xml`'s `<application>` tag for dev builds only |\n| `Requested internal only, but not enough space` when installing APK | Pre-installed apps on the AVD consumed 95%+ of `/data` | Wipe data: kill emulator, relaunch with `-wipe-data` flag. Re-install. |\n| Bundle loads but renders nothing — Lynx logs `Error: WebSocket is not found` | Used a dev-mode rspeedy bundle (which has webpack-dev-transport HMR client) | Build with `npx rspeedy build --mode production` for asset bundling |\n| Bundle URL points at rspeedy dev server and host shows `com.lynx.error error 201` | Dev server injects the HMR client; embedded runtime doesn't ship `LynxWebSocketModule` | Set `environments.lynx.dev.hmr: false, liveReload: false` in `lynx.config.ts` and restart the dev server (see `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #7) |\n| `OnPatchFinishForFiber` fires but `uiautomator dump` shows only `FrameLayout`/`LinearLayout` | The ExpoView child is rendered but not measured → never drawn to the framebuffer | The `shouldUseAndroidLayout = true` fix from Step 2 |\n| Lynx image fetches fail with `onFailed src:/static/image/...` | Production rspeedy bundle doesn't include `static/` images in the APK | Either ship images via a CDN and reference by URL, or write the asset path into `LynxTemplateProvider.loadFromAssets` |\n| Hermes logcat is silent about the demo | Logcat tags filter excluded `lynx` tag | Use `--pid=$(adb shell pidof <pkg>)` to scope logcat to the app process |\n| Jest reports `Could not locate module ./modules/<x>-view/src` mapped as mock path | `moduleNameMapper` regex has no path-prefix anchor, doesn't match relative `./modules/...` imports | Use `(.*/)?modules/<x>-view/src$` (anchored with `.*/` prefix) |\n| After a pnpm workspace restructure: `Cannot find module 'lynx-view'` even though tests previously passed | The moduleNameMapper only covers `<pkg>/src$`, but tests import `from '<pkg>'` (resolved via package.json `main`). You need TWO aliases. | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #23. Add `'(.*/)?lynx-view$'` alongside the `src$` alias. Don't cut either without `grep -rn` proving no import path needs it. |\n| Jest tests have 20+ TS errors: `Cannot find name 'describe' / 'it' / 'expect'` | `@types/jest` not in `tsconfig.json` `types[]` | Add `\"types\": [\"jest\"]` to `compilerOptions`, or extend `jest-expo`'s preset which already includes it |\n| Consumer writes `onLoad={(e) => console.log(e.url)}` and gets `undefined` | Type signature is `(error: payload) => void` but RN wraps events in `{ nativeEvent: payload }` | Type as `(event: { nativeEvent: payload }) => void`; consumer reads `event.nativeEvent.url` |\n| `EventDispatcher` type mismatch on `Map<String, Any?>` | Kotlin's `mapOf()` infers `Map`, not `MutableMap`; the spread boundary doesn't auto-coerce | Declare `EventDispatcher<MutableMap<String, Any?>>()` and call with `mutableMapOf(...)` |\n| `<LynxView testID=\"x\">` doesn't propagate to native | `LynxViewProps` doesn't extend `ViewProps` | Add `& Omit<ViewProps, 'style' \\| 'children'>` to the props type |\n| Build warning `Unsupported property \"font-variant-numeric\" was removed` | Lynx template encoder strips `font-variant-numeric` at encode time | Use a monospace `font-family` instead; don't expect proportional fonts to align numerals |\n| Physical Android device not in Argent `list-devices` | Argent is iOS-simulator + Chromium-aware; doesn't enumerate physical Android devices | Use raw `adb -s <serial>` for physical Android work; reserve Argent for iOS sims |\n| iOS `LynxView` lays out at `0×0` or its default size despite JS `style={{flex:1}}` | iOS does not auto-inherit parent constraints the way Android's `shouldUseAndroidLayout=true` does — the consumer must set `setLayoutWidthMode/.exact` etc. explicitly | See `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md`. Set the modes in `required init` + reassert in `layoutSubviews`. |\n| iOS host LogBox shows `com.lynx.error error 201` with no message, even though Lynx has the actual JS error | `lynxView(_:didRecieveError:)` and the network/HTTP error path emit `NSError.localizedDescription` directly, throwing away `userInfo` keys (`reason`, `NSDebugDescriptionErrorKey`, and the nested `NSUnderlyingErrorKey` chain). The host only ever sees the synthesized \"operation couldn't be completed\" copy. | Read `userInfo` keys in one shared helper (recursive on `NSUnderlyingErrorKey`, fall through to `reason` → `NSDebugDescriptionErrorKey` → `localizedDescription`) and forward `\"\\(nsError.code)\"` as `code` — the integer is what Lynx emits. Same helper for both `didRecieveError` and any fetch/HTTP failure path so the two error routes can't drift. See `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` \"Error translation — don't lose the userInfo chain\". |\n| iOS `__weak typeof()` compile errors across multiple Lynx `.mm` files (`LynxSVGRenderer.mm`, `SRWebSocket.m`, `LynxWebSocket.m`, `DevTool*.mm`) on Xcode 26 + RN 0.86 | `typeof` is a Clang GNU extension; Xcode 26's default `-std=c++20` doesn't include it. ARC is also off in some per-file overrides. | `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` \"Xcode 26 + Lynx 4.0 + RN 0.86\" section has the full 3-part fix (Podfile `post_install` hook + per-file `COMPILER_FLAGS` sed). The 2-flag combo `-fobjc-arc -std=gnu++20` is the minimum viable fix; either alone is insufficient. **Critical:** the per-file pbxproj sed must run in the same shell command as `pod install` (prepended in the consumer's `ios` npm script). Putting it in `post_install` fails silently because CocoaPods writes pbxproj AFTER the hook returns. |\n| iOS podspec `s.resources = \"main.bundle\"` shipped the wrong bundle to every consumer app | Library podspecs that ship a bundle resource embed *the library's* bundle in *every* consumer — which is correct only when the pod IS the consumer or is a dedicated delivery pod | See `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` Path A caveat. Libraries don't own the bundle; consumer apps own their own. Have the consumer app drop the bundle via Path B or its own build script. |\n| `tsc --noEmit` flags `Cannot find name 'process'/'Buffer'/'__dirname'` after adding `\"types\": [\"jest\"]` | `types` is an allowlist, not an addition — adding jest auto-gates node/react-native ambient types | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #21. Either drop `types` and use a separate `tsconfig.test.json`, or list every ambient type you need. |\n| `git reset HEAD <file>` unstaged unrelated edits in a restructured workspace | `git reset` matches by pathspec; after a monorepo move/rename, the spec can resolve to more than you intended | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #22. Prefer `git restore --staged <pathspec>`; after restructures, re-stage by directory not `git add -A`. |\n| `path.resolve(__dirname, '../../../...')` resolves to the wrong directory | `__dirname` is the *script file's* directory, not `process.cwd()`. Counting parent hops from cwd gives the wrong depth | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #24. From `apps/demo/scripts/foo.js`, the workspace root is `../../../../` (4 hops), not `../../`. Print `console.log(path.resolve(__dirname, '...'))` once to verify before relying on it. |\n| Chokidar `add` event never fires for an existing file when you set `ignoreInitial: false` | `ignoreInitial: false` waits for the watcher's `ready` event before emitting; if `ready` is blocked (or the file already exists), the listener may never see `add` | See `references/lynx-4.0-gotchas.md` #25. Combine `ignoreInitial: true` (skip existing files) with an explicit one-shot copy at the top of the script. The copy is the deterministic initial sync; chokidar handles only subsequent changes. |\n| Library podspec ships `s.resources = \"main.bundle\"` and ends up embedding your bundle in their APK | The podspec's `s.resources` adds the file to every consumer app's main bundle at `pod install` time — but the bundle is per-app state, not library state | See `references/lynx-4.0-ios.md` \"Path A caveat — LIBRARY ANTI-PATTERN\". Remove the `s.resources` line from the library podspec entirely. The consumer app's `lynx:build` script copies the bundle to the consumer's own Xcode Copy Bundle Resources phase. |\n\n## Verification\n\n| Check | Command | Pass criterion |\n|---|---|---|\n| APK builds | `cd android && ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease` | `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` |\n| Install succeeds | `adb install -r app-release.apk` | `Success` (no \"not enough space\") |\n| App launches | `adb shell monkey -p <pkg> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1` | `Events injected: 1` |\n| Bundle loads | `adb logcat -d --pid=$(adb shell pidof <pkg>) \\| grep 'dispatchLoadSuccess templateSize'` | Line shows `templateSize: <bytes>` matching the bundled file size |\n| UI paints | `uiautomator dump` + grep for `ScrollView` | Contains `android.widget.ScrollView` or `HorizontalScrollView` |\n| Screen has content | `identify -format '%[mean]' /tmp/screencap.png` | Mean < 64000 (white = 65535). **Caveat:** for templates with mostly-white backgrounds (e.g. minimal Lynx demo pages), mean stays near 62000 even when content rendered correctly. Trust the ScrollView check above as the primary signal; the pixel mean is only meaningful when the expected content has substantial non-white area. |\n| Tests pass | `npx jest` | All 4+ tests green, no skipped |\n| No crash | `adb logcat -d --pid=$(adb shell pidof <pkg>) \\| grep 'FATAL EXCEPTION'` | Empty result |\n\n## Test pattern\n\n```ts\n// __tests__/App.test.tsx\nimport { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react-native';\nimport { LynxView } from '../modules/<engine>-view/mock';\n\ndescribe('LynxView events', () => {\n  it('fires onLoad with nativeEvent shape', async () => {\n    const onLoad = jest.fn();\n    render(<LynxView src=\"main.lynx.bundle\" onLoad={onLoad} />);\n    await waitFor(() => expect(onLoad).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1));\n    const [event] = onLoad.mock.calls[0];\n    expect(event.nativeEvent).toEqual({ url: 'main.lynx.bundle' });\n  });\n\n  it('fires onError with structured LynxErrorEvent', async () => {\n    const onError = jest.fn();\n    render(<LynxView src=\"\" onError={onError} />);\n    await waitFor(() => expect(onError).toHaveBeenCalled());\n    const [event] = onError.mock.calls[0];\n    expect(event.nativeEvent).toMatchObject({ code: expect.any(Number), level: 'error' });\n  });\n});\n```\n\nThe Jest mock at `modules/<engine>-view/mock.tsx` simulates the native bridge — `useEffect` fires `onLoad` on mount with non-empty `src`, fires `onError` with the structured `LynxErrorEvent` shape when `src` is empty. Verify the mock matches the real native payload shape, otherwise tests pass but the real device fails.\n\n## When to Extend vs Create a New Skill\n\nExtend this skill if the new learning is:\n- Another Lynx 4.0 API surface (lifecycle events, message bridge, runtime APIs)\n- Another Expo Modules Core gotcha that's also non-obvious\n- Another dependency conflict (Fresco, image service, WebSocket, etc.)\n\nCreate a sibling skill if the new learning is:\n- A different engine entirely (Weex, mini-program runtime, WebView-as-engine)\n- A different transport (React Native New Architecture, bridgeless mode, fabric)\n- Production-grade concerns (splash, error boundary, OTA updates of bundles)\n\nThe `react-native-mini-app-architecture` skill covers \"should you\" decisions. ```tsx // app/_layout.tsx — let Expo Router/native stack own screens import { Stack } from 'expo-router'; export default function Layout() { return <Stack screenOptions={{ gestureEnabled: true }} />; } ``` Yes, iOS swipe-back works when each route is a native Expo Router/React Navigation stack screen containing an `<ExpoLynxView />`. If `react-router` runs **inside one Lynx bundle**, native sees only one screen, so native swipe-back is impossible. You would need a custom Lynx pan gesture + `history.back()`, which is not recommended. Current example has no router installed; add Expo Router only when moving navigation to the RN host.

The Lynx repo confirms swipe-back is possible, but it is implemented by the **native container**, not `react-router-dom`: - `LynxViewShellViewController.m:487` adds `UIScreenEdgePanGestureRecognizer`. - `LynxViewShellViewController.m:565` drives the interactive animation. - `LynxViewShellViewController.m:620` commits the native stack close. - `LynxNavigator.h:40` exposes `onNavigateBack` for native swipe-back. - `NavigationHost.swift:61` disables UIKit’s default gesture because Explorer owns a custom native stack. Recommended for Expo: ```tsx // Native screen stack owns navigation and swipe-back. <Stack.Screen name="lynx-detail" /> // Each screen renders its own <ExpoLynxView />. ``` `react-router-dom` routes inside one Lynx view are only virtual pages, so UIKit cannot swipe between them. Skipped copying Explorer’s custom gesture; use Expo Router/native stack unless each Lynx route must remain inside one view.
Reasoning
**Confirming legacy and new navigation handling differences** **Outlining ExpoLynxView back gesture integration options** **Proposing minimal ExpoLynxView navigation architecture**

{"success": true, "name": "systematic-debugging", "description": "4-phase root cause debugging: understand bugs before fixing.", "tags": ["debugging", "troubleshooting", "problem-solving", "root-cause", "investigation"], "related_skills": ["test-driven-development", "plan", "subagent-driven-development"], "content": "---\nname: systematic-debugging\ndescription: \"4-phase root cause debugging: understand bugs before fixing.\"\nversion: 1.1.0\nauthor: Hermes Agent (adapted from obra/superpowers)\nlicense: MIT\nplatforms: [linux, macos, windows]\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [debugging, troubleshooting, problem-solving, root-cause, investigation]\n    related_skills: [test-driven-development, plan, subagent-driven-development]\n---\n\n# Systematic Debugging\n\n## Overview\n\nRandom fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.\n\n**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.\n\n**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**\n\n## The Iron Law\n\n```\nNO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST\n```\n\nIf you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.\n\n## The Feedback Loop Rule\n\nThe feedback loop is the debugging work. Before reading code to build a theory, create or identify a **tight** command that can go red on the user's exact symptom and green when the bug is fixed. A tight loop is fast, deterministic, agent-runnable, and specific enough to catch this bug — not merely \"doesn't crash\".\n\nWhen a clean repro is hard, spend disproportionate effort building the loop. Guessing without a red-capable loop is the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.\n\n## When to Use\n\nUse for ANY technical issue:\n- Test failures\n- Bugs in production\n- Unexpected behavior\n- Performance problems\n- Build failures\n- Integration issues\n\n**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**\n- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)\n- \"Just one quick fix\" seems obvious\n- You've already tried multiple fixes\n- Previous fix didn't work\n- You don't fully understand the issue\n\n**Don't skip when:**\n- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)\n- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)\n- Someone wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)\n\n## The Four Phases\n\nYou MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation\n\n**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**\n\n### 1. Read Error Messages Carefully\n\n- Don't skip past errors or warnings\n- They often contain the exact solution\n- Read stack traces completely\n- Note line numbers, file paths, error codes\n\n**Action:** Use `read_file` on the relevant source files. Use `search_files` to find the error string in the codebase.\n\n### 2. Build a Tight Feedback Loop\n\n- Can you trigger the user's exact symptom with one command?\n- Does the command fail for this bug and only pass once the bug is fixed?\n- Is it fast enough to run repeatedly?\n- Is it deterministic? For flaky bugs, can you raise the reproduction rate high enough to debug?\n- If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess.\n\n**Ways to construct a loop — try in roughly this order:**\n\n1. **Failing test** at the seam that reaches the bug: unit, integration, or end-to-end.\n2. **HTTP script / curl** against a running dev server.\n3. **CLI invocation** with fixture input, diffing stdout/stderr against expected output.\n4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright/Puppeteer) asserting on DOM, console, or network.\n5. **Replay a captured trace**: HAR, request payload, event log, queue message, or webhook body.\n6. **Throwaway harness** that boots the smallest useful slice of the system and calls the failing path.\n7. **Property / fuzz loop** when the bug is intermittent wrong output over a broad input space.\n8. **Bisection harness** suitable for `git bisect run` when the bug appeared between two known states.\n9. **Differential loop** comparing old vs new version, two configs, two providers, or two datasets.\n10. **Human-in-the-loop script** only as a last resort: script the human steps and capture their result so the loop stays structured.\n\n**Tighten the loop once it exists:**\n\n- Make it faster: cache setup, narrow scope, skip unrelated initialization.\n- Make the signal sharper: assert the exact symptom, not generic success.\n- Make it more deterministic: pin time, seed randomness, isolate filesystem, freeze network.\n\nFor non-deterministic bugs, the immediate goal is a higher reproduction rate, not perfection. Run the trigger 100x, parallelize, add stress, narrow timing windows, or inject sleeps. A 50% flake is debuggable; a 1% flake usually is not.\n\n**Action:** Use the `terminal` tool to run the tight loop:\n\n```bash\n# Run a specific failing test\npytest tests/test_module.py::test_name -v\n\n# Or run a scripted repro\npython scripts/repro_bug.py\n\n# Or run a high-repetition flaky repro\nfor i in {1..100}; do pytest tests/test_flake.py::test_name -q || break; done\n```\n\n### 3. Check Recent Changes\n\n- What changed that could cause this?\n- Git diff, recent commits\n- New dependencies, config changes\n\n**Action:**\n\n```bash\n# Recent commits\ngit log --oneline -10\n\n# Uncommitted changes\ngit diff\n\n# Changes in specific file\ngit log -p --follow src/problematic_file.py | head -100\n```\n\n### 4. Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems\n\n**WHEN system has multiple components (API → service → database, CI → build → deploy):**\n\n**BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**\n\nFor EACH component boundary:\n- Log what data enters the component\n- Log what data exits the component\n- Verify environment/config propagation\n- Check state at each layer\n\nRun once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks.\nTHEN analyze evidence to identify the failing component.\nTHEN investigate that specific component.\n\n### 5. Trace Data Flow\n\n**WHEN error is deep in the call stack:**\n\n- Where does the bad value originate?\n- What called this function with the bad value?\n- Keep tracing upstream until you find the source\n- Fix at the source, not at the symptom\n\n**Action:** Use `search_files` to trace references:\n\n```python\n# Find where the function is called\nsearch_files(\"function_name(\", path=\"src/\", file_glob=\"*.py\")\n\n# Find where the variable is set\nsearch_files(\"variable_name\\\\s*=\", path=\"src/\", file_glob=\"*.py\")\n```\n\n### Phase 1 Completion Checklist\n\n- [ ] Error messages fully read and understood\n- [ ] A tight loop command exists and has been run at least once\n- [ ] Loop is red-capable: it asserts the user's exact symptom, not a nearby failure\n- [ ] Loop is deterministic, or a flaky bug has a high enough reproduction rate to debug\n- [ ] Recent changes identified and reviewed\n- [ ] Evidence gathered (logs, state, data flow)\n- [ ] Problem isolated to specific component/code\n- [ ] Root cause hypotheses can be stated and tested\n\n**STOP:** Do not proceed to Phase 2 until you understand WHY it's happening.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 2: Pattern Analysis\n\n**Find the pattern before fixing:**\n\n### 0. Minimize the Reproduction\n\nOnce the loop is red, shrink the repro to the smallest scenario that still goes red. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut. Keep only what is load-bearing for the failure.\n\nDone when removing any remaining element makes the loop go green. A minimal repro narrows the hypothesis space and often becomes the cleanest regression test.\n\n### 1. Find Working Examples\n\n- Locate similar working code in the same codebase\n- What works that's similar to what's broken?\n\n**Action:** Use `search_files` to find comparable patterns:\n\n```python\nsearch_files(\"similar_pattern\", path=\"src/\", file_glob=\"*.py\")\n```\n\n### 2. Compare Against References\n\n- If implementing a pattern, read the reference implementation COMPLETELY\n- Don't skim — read every line\n- Understand the pattern fully before applying\n\n### 3. Identify Differences\n\n- What's different between working and broken?\n- List every difference, however small\n- Don't assume \"that can't matter\"\n\n### 4. Understand Dependencies\n\n- What other components does this need?\n- What settings, config, environment?\n- What assumptions does it make?\n\n---\n\n## Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing\n\n**Scientific method:**\n\n### 1. Form Ranked Falsifiable Hypotheses\n\n- Generate 3–5 plausible hypotheses before testing any single one.\n- Rank them by likelihood and cheapness to falsify.\n- State the prediction each hypothesis makes: \"If X is the cause, then changing or observing Y should make Z happen.\"\n- Discard or sharpen any hypothesis that does not make a testable prediction.\n\nIf the user is present, show the ranked list before testing. They may have domain knowledge that instantly re-ranks it. If the user is AFK, proceed with your ranking.\n\n### 2. Test Minimally\n\n- Test the highest-ranked hypothesis with the smallest possible probe.\n- Change one variable at a time.\n- Don't fix multiple things at once.\n- Prefer debugger/REPL inspection when available; one breakpoint beats ten logs.\n- If you add logs, tag every temporary line with a unique prefix such as `[DEBUG-a4f2]` so cleanup is a single search.\n\n### 3. Verify Before Continuing\n\n- Did it work? → Phase 4\n- Didn't work? → Form NEW hypothesis\n- DON'T add more fixes on top\n\n### 4. When You Don't Know\n\n- Say \"I don't understand X\"\n- Don't pretend to know\n- Ask the user for help\n- Research more\n\n---\n\n## Phase 4: Implementation\n\n**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**\n\n### 1. Create Failing Test Case\n\n- Simplest possible reproduction\n- Automated test if possible\n- MUST have before fixing\n- Use the `test-driven-development` skill\n\n### 2. Implement Single Fix\n\n- Address the root cause identified\n- ONE change at a time\n- No \"while I'm here\" improvements\n- No bundled refactoring\n\n### 3. Verify Fix\n\n```bash\n# Run the specific regression test\npytest tests/test_module.py::test_regression -v\n\n# Run full suite — no regressions\npytest tests/ -q\n```\n\n### 4. If Fix Doesn't Work — The Rule of Three\n\n- **STOP.**\n- Count: How many fixes have you tried?\n- If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information\n- **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**\n- DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion\n\n### 5. Return to Phase 1.**\n\n**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (Phase 4 step 5).\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Issue is simple, don't need process\" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |\n| \"Emergency, no time for process\" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |\n| \"Just try this first, then investigate\" | First fix sets the pattern. This allows you to position your content appropriately around notches, status bars, home indicators, and other such device and operating system interface elements. It also provides a `SafeAreaView` component that you can use in place of `View` to automatically inset your views to account for safe areas.\n\n## Installation\n\nTerminal\n\n`-``npx`\n\nIf you are installing this in an [existing React Native app](/bare/overview), make sure to [install `expo`](/bare/installing-expo-modules) in your project. This is a more advanced use-case, and might perform worse than `SafeAreaView` when rotating the device.\n\nExample\n\n```\n\n\nimport{ useSafeAreaInsets }{} from'react-native-safe-area-context'; function HookComponent HookComponent(){const = useSafeAreaInsets(); return<View style={{ paddingTop: insets.top }} /><View< View style ={{ paddingTop: insets.top }} ={{paddingTop:. top}}/>;}\n\n\n```\n\nReturns\n\n[`EdgeInsets`](/versions/v57.0.0/sdk/safe-area-context#edgeinsets)\n\n## Types\n\n### `Edge`\n\nString union of possible edges.\n\nAcceptable values are: `'top'`, `'right'`, `'bottom'`, `'left'`.\n\n### `EdgeInsets`\n\nRepresent the hook result.\n\nEdgeInsets Properties\n\n| Name | Type | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `bottom` | `number` | Value of bottom inset. |\n| `left` | `number` | Value of left inset. |\n| `right` | `number` | Value of right inset. |\n| `top` | `number` | Value of top inset. |\n\n## Guides\n\n### Context\n\nTo use safe area context, you need to add `SafeAreaProvider` in your app root component.\n\n> You may need to add it in other places too, including at the root of any modals any routes when using `react-native-screen`.\n\n```\n\n\nimport{ SafeAreaProvider }{SafeAreaProvider} from'react-native-safe-area-context'; function App App(){return<SafeAreaProvider><SafeAreaProvider< SafeAreaProvider>...SafeAreaProvider>; } SafeAreaProvider> SafeAreaProvider SafeAreaProvider>;}\n\n\n```\n\nThen, you can use [`useSafeAreaInsets()`](/versions/v57.0.0/sdk/safe-area-context#usesafeareainsets) hook and also consumer API to access inset data:\n\n```\n\n\nimport{ SafeAreaInsetsContext }{SafeAreaInsetsContext} from'react-native-safe-area-context'; function Component Component(){return(<SafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer><SafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer<SafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer>  {insets =><View style={{ paddingTop: insets.top }} /><View< View style ={{ paddingTop: insets.top }} ={{paddingTop:. top}}/>}  SafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer> ); } SafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer>SafeAreaInsetsContext.ConsumerSafeAreaInsetsContext.Consumer>);}\n\n\n```\n\n### Optimization\n\nIf you can, use `SafeAreaView`. It's implemented natively so when rotating the device, there is no delay from the asynchronous bridge.\n\nTo speed up the initial render, you can import `initialWindowMetrics` from this package and set as the `initialMetrics` prop on the provider as described in Web SSR. You cannot do this if your provider remounts, or you are using `react-native-navigation`.\n\n```\n\n\nimport{ SafeAreaProvider, initialWindowMetrics }{SafeAreaProvider,} from'react-native-safe-area-context'; function App App(){return<SafeAreaProvider initialMetrics={initialWindowMetrics}><SafeAreaProvider< SafeAreaProvider initialMetrics ={initialWindowMetrics} ={}>...SafeAreaProvider>; } SafeAreaProvider> SafeAreaProvider SafeAreaProvider>;}\n\n\n```\n\n### Web SSR\n\nIf you are doing server side rendering on the web, you can use `initialSafeAreaInsets` to inject values based on the device the user has, or simply pass zero. Otherwise, insets measurement will break rendering your page content since it is async.\n\n### Migrating from CSS\n\n#### Before\n\nIn a web-only app, you would use CSS environment variables to get the size of the screen's safe area insets.\n\nstyles.css\n\n```\n\n\ndiv{padding-top: env();padding-left: env();padding-bottom: env();padding-right: env();}\n\n\n```\n\n#### After\n\nUniversally, the hook `useSafeAreaInsets()` can provide access to this information.\n\nApp.js\n\n```\n\n\nimport{ useSafeAreaInsets }{} from'react-native-safe-area-context'; function App App(){const = useSafeAreaInsets(); return(<View style={{ paddingTop: insets.top, paddingLeft: insets.left, paddingBottom: insets.bottom, paddingRight: insets.right, }} /><View< View style ={{ paddingTop: insets.top, paddingLeft: insets.left, paddingBottom: insets.bottom, paddingRight: insets.right, }} ={{paddingTop:. top, paddingLeft:. left, paddingBottom:. bottom, paddingRight:. right,}}/>);}\n\n\n```",

        "title": "Understanding Layout - Lynx",
        "description": ", are used for aligning elements. The position property, along with left, right, top, bottom properties, are used to position elements. direction and logical properties are used to support the internationalization of layouts. For the layout properties supported by Lynx with the same name in the Web, the behavior of these properties will be consistent with those in the Web.\n\nmin-width, max-height, min-height, margin, padding, and border-width to describe the size and box model of an element. These properties support various length units such as px, %, vh and etc. Additionally, width and height support max-content and fit-content for sizing elements according to their content.  box-sizing is border-box by default and Lynx does not exhibit the behavior of margin collapsing. By default, the size properties of Lynx, such as width, height, and max-width, describe the size of the border box.\n\nthe grid layout, a layout in the Web that can divide the space into a two-dimensional grid and place elements in the specified rows and columns. Lynx supports a subset of its features.  Relative Layout If you want to describe the layout through the relative position relationship between elements, you can set the display property to relative and use the relative layout. The relative layout(inspired by Android’s Relative Layout) can declare the layout by describing the position relationship between elements (for example, one element is located to the left of another element).\n\nText and Inline Layout In Lynx, text cannot be directly inserted into the <view> element, and the display property of Lynx does not support the values of inline and block.",

        "description": "elements such as text and images, presented in different layouts to create diverse page styles. This section aims to help everyone understand how to construct the most basic views. Element tag: UI Building Blocks Lynx defines content and structure using a markup language, with the most basic unit being an element tag. The concept of an element tag is similar to HTML elements, which can be used to encapsulate different parts of the content to present or operate in a specific manner.\n\nsource code can be used to display a piece of text:  < text >Hello Lynx</ text >\nAnatomy of an Element tag The basic usage of element tags is very similar to HTML elements:  Each element tag consists of the following parts: Start tag: Includes the name of the element tag (in this case, text) surrounded by angle brackets, indicating where the element tag begins. End tag: Similar to the start tag but includes a forward slash before the element tag’s name, indicating where the element tag ends.\n\nFor example, each element tag can use attributes such as style and class to set background, border-radius, shadow styles, and support some CSS syntax. The following code sets the background color of an element tag to red:  < text style = \"background:red;\" >Hello Lynx</ text >\nIn this example, style is the attribute name, and background:red is the attribute value. For more attributes, refer to the API Reference.\n\nView The <view> is the most basic element, commonly used to wrap other elements and carry some drawing capability. Simulator works because `LynxEnv` initializes after its key window exists, so `env(safe-area-inset-*)` receives valid values. On the physical app, Expo initializes `LynxEnv` earlier; `LynxEnv.mm:515-528` reads the key window only once, gets `nil`/zero insets, and keeps those process-global values. Correction: Lynx supports CSS `env()`. The applied `globalProps` fix avoids this startup-timing bug by reading each actual `ExpoLynxView.safeAreaInsets` whenever they change.
